title: Mind training
hookLine: the slogans of Atisha's tradition, such as "drive all blames into one"

lines: A STICKY NOTE ON THE MIRROR.
A LINE FOR THE HARD MOMENT.
cards: A sticky note on the mirror. A magnet on the fridge. A line written on the inside of a wrist.
People keep short sentences where they'll bump into them, because a long book won't be there at the moment you snap at your kid or your coworker.
Tibetan Buddhists have a whole set of lines like that, handed down for centuries. One of them sounds almost rude at first: drive all blames into one.

teach.b: Lojong. Lo is mind; jong means training, or cleaning up. Tibetans trace the teachings to Atisha, the Bengali master who came to Tibet from India.
There's a story people tell about him: he brought along a cranky servant who argued with everything, because he needed someone to practice patience on.

When he heard how kind the Tibetans were, he wondered if he'd still need the servant. Later, a teacher named Geshe Chekawa gathered the teachings into short slogans, meant to be memorized and carried. Some are gentle.
Be grateful to everyone. Always keep a joyful mind. Some are sharp.
Don't wait in ambush. Don't talk about other people's faults. And then: drive all blames into one.
Teachers explain that it does not mean blame yourself for everything.
The one is self-cherishing: the habit that puts me at the center of every story, then feels outraged when the world doesn't cooperate.

So when something goes wrong, instead of scanning the room for someone to blame, you look at the grasping in your own reaction. That's where the heat is coming from, and it's the one thing you can actually work with.
It doesn't excuse harm, and it doesn't mean staying where you're hurt.
It means your own mind is the training ground. Be grateful to everyone fits the same way: the difficult coworker is Atisha's cranky servant, giving you something to practice on.
Teachers suggest carrying just one slogan at a time, and letting it meet the day. One slogan.

how: Tibetan Buddhists study the lojong slogans, often in Geshe Chekawa's Seven-Point Mind Training, memorize them, and bring one slogan at a time into daily situations, especially difficult ones.

o: training the mind with short slogans
a long scripture memorized by monks
a set of rules for meditation posture

games.q: match the pieces of mind training.
p: brought a cranky servant to practice on

s: 'drive all blames into one' means blame yourself for everything
the one is self-cherishing, not your worth as a person.
Geshe Chekawa gathered the teachings into short slogans
they were meant to be memorized and carried into the day.
the slogan means staying where you're being harmed
it doesn't excuse harm; it makes your own reaction the place to work.

games.q: someone cuts in front of you in a long line and you're fuming. the slogan says drive all blames into one. which one?
o: the self-cherishing in your own reaction.
games.why: teachers say the one is self-cherishing: the habit that puts me at the center. that's where the heat comes from, and where the work is.

practice: Choose one slogan to carry, drive all blames into one, be grateful to everyone, or always keep a joyful mind, whichever pinches a little, and say it silently once.
Sit with the breath, and when a thought or an irritation comes, let the line and the moment meet, without forcing an answer.

wordCard.voice: Lojong. Mind training: short slogans from Atisha's tradition, carried into the day so the hard moments become the practice.

orig.note: Tibetan blo sbyong: blo (mind) + sbyong (to train, to purify).

carryVoice: Your line: one slogan. Short enough to be there when the hard moment comes. Until tomorrow.
